idiom_name: discriminated command payload + point-to-point channel + single-owner handler registry
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define the operation as data (a type tag plus parameters), wrap it in the message envelope whose headers carry routing, correlation, expiry and reply metadata, and send it on a point-to-point channel whose contract is one receiver per command. The receiver is an endpoint that deserializes, validates the discriminator and dispatches through a registry (type -> handler) to the single component that owns the state. Keep the tag explicit and versioned, decide the idempotency/deduplication policy before going live, and add a reply channel only when the caller genuinely needs the outcome.
code_sketch:
command = { "type": "reserve-stock", "order_id": "A-17", "qty": 2 }
channel("reserve-stock").send(command, headers={ "message_id": mid, "reply_to": None })
# receiver:
handler = registry[command["type"]]            # unknown type -> dead-letter channel
handler.execute(command, context)              # idempotent, single owner of the state
pitfalls: A command that mirrors the receiver's internal methods (setter-style, one command per column) couples the two sides as tightly as the remote call the pattern was meant to avoid.
No discriminator, or no policy for unknown types: the command is silently dropped or matched to the wrong handler.
Assuming exactly-once semantics: without idempotency or deduplication an at-least-once channel executes the command twice.

Wrong move: replace a synchronous call with a command queue without reassigning who owns completion -> failure: the publish succeeds, the consumer fails or lags, and nobody notices because the caller stopped caring and no one was made responsible for the outcome -> instead: make completion ownership explicit - consumer acks, dead-letter alerts and an idempotent handler on the receiver side, or a correlated reply channel when the caller must know the result.

Wrong move: watch only producer-side metrics (messages sent) -> failure: consumer lag, handler error rate and dead-letter growth climb while the sender still reports success -> instead: treat consumer throughput, lag and DLQ depth as the command's real success signal and alert on them.

Wrong move: let publishers post to an unbounded command queue with no admission control -> failure: during spikes producers outrun consumers, latency and broker memory grow until workers or the broker collapse -> instead: bound the queue, choose block/reject/shed explicitly, and rate-limit producers when lag crosses a threshold.
